ch48.anchor: a poet named Fujiwara no Ietaka
ch48.note: Fujiwara no Ietaka (1158–1237), one of the great poets of his age and a compiler, under the retired Emperor Go-Toba, of the Shin-Kokin Wakashū (1205), the eighth imperial waka anthology. By tradition he spent his last years on this hill above the sea at Naniwa (old Osaka) practicing nissokan, the “sun-contemplation” — the first of the sixteen meditations of the Contemplation Sutra, in which one gazes at the setting sun to fix the mind on Amida Buddha’s Pure Land in the west. The spot took its name, Yūhigaoka (“Hill of the Evening Sun”), from the practice, and the mound they find is his reputed grave; the death-poem quoted just below is the one attached to him by this tradition.

A gorintō, a stone memorial built in five stacked stones — cube, sphere, pyramid, half-moon, and jewel — for the five elements of Buddhist cosmology (earth, water, fire, wind, and the void). Common as a grave-marker from the Heian and Kamakura periods on, it is the form of Ietaka’s reputed tomb here; the stone is read “Karyū-zuka,” a Sino-Japanese reading of the same characters that spell his name.

Danna-sama, “master” or “husband,” is the deferential word a wife uses for the man of her house. That Toshizō — a bachelor of thirty-four who has never been anyone’s husband — confesses to having dreamed since boyhood of being addressed by this one word, and gently scolds Oyuki the next morning for leaving it off, is the quiet heart of the chapter.
